Thank you very much, Your Excellency the Vice President of ECOSOC, Excellencies, colleagues. My apologies for coming late. We have just begun the work of the Beyond GDP outcome of the Pact of the Future, and I believe that will be an exciting input into the work that we do to accelerate work on the Agenda 2030. Excellencies, we come together today following a hallmark year of the Resident Coordinator System and entities across the UN Development Group. As we heard from the Secretary-General yesterday in the presentation of his report, This year has pressed the development system, and we know the year ahead will be even more testing. Six years into the repositioning, we have a Resident Coordinator System that is delivering for those we serve, and we know that this support is needed now more than ever. And the UN system needs to come together in a coordinated, cohesive manner to provide this support. Around the world, people are confronting a convergence of crises.— entrenched conflict, economic instability, persistent poverty and inequalities, constrained multilateralism, and declining support for development funding and financing. This is precisely the moment in which we must recommit to accelerated action that delivers the Sustainable Development Goals for people and planet, as guided by the roadmap that the 2024 QCPR has set. The UN Development System, with the leadership of Resident Coordinators, is redoubling its efforts to align with Member States' expectations, while finding ways to do so more effectively. I am grateful for the leadership that Member States have shown in continuing to guide our work. Excellencies, my Annual Report tells the story of a UN Development System constantly in motion—resilient, adaptive, ambitious, and firmly anchored in countries' needs. UN teams are delivering—in countries beset by crisis or in communities facing down persistent poverty and inequalities. In 2024, 98% of host governments reported that the UN's activities, as articulated in the cooperation frameworks, were closely aligned with national priorities. 93% of our host governments indicated that RCs and UN country teams provided support for changes in national policies and regulatory frameworks to advance all the SDGs.— a 7% increase over the previous year. 90% of contributing countries agree that the RC system has scaled up collective action for the SDGs. And 84% agree that the RC system helped improve coherence in UN activities and in reducing the duplication of efforts. These are more than numbers. They represent a shift in how we work together as a UN system. And the RC system is the engine of this accelerated support two countries. First, Resident Coordinators are leveraging national and global processes to boost systems transformation for SDG acceleration. Cooperation frameworks increasingly embed integrated approaches on the priorities agreed with governments. They are maximizing interventions across multiple SDGs to amplify the impact and ground international commitments in countries. RCs and our UN country teams spearheaded over 100 national initiatives with governments to leverage the Summit of the Future to accelerate SDG implementation. Second, from civil society to financial institutions, Resident Coordinators are convening the partnerships that scale impact and sustain the results. Notably, with international financial institutions— is growing collaboration with international financial institutions is growing, with 73% of UN country teams reporting active engagement with our IFIs. 90% of host governments reported that Resident Coordinators have helped to leverage partnerships in support of national SDG efforts. Third, Resident Coordinators play a key role in channeling global and country-level sources of funding that incentivize joint work and unlocking financing for SDG solutions. The Joint SDG Fund has been the main muscle behind the Resident Coordinators' efforts to foster joint, transformative, and coherent programming. In 2024, the Fund supported RCs and UN teams to initiate 136 new joint programs across 90 countries in transformative areas such as food systems, energy, digitalization, jobs, and social protection. Cumulatively, the Fund has reached over 206 million people and catalyzed $1.6 billion in investments. Fourth, the Resident Coordinator System is guiding the UN Country Teams to deliver development results and enable the realization of efficiencies. Resident Coordinators track implementation of the Business Operations Strategy, negotiate arrangements for common premises, facilitate common back offices, and promote the shift towards global service centres. Fifth, the Resident Coordinator System is fostering increased accountability and transparency for results. They are spearheading efforts to strengthen the accountability to Member States, including by providing comprehensive result reports, and improve the use of digital platforms for sharing information on the work of UN country teams. Excellencies, Some of you may be familiar with this positive legacy of the repositioning. However, there are some notable shifts in the past year. Member States responded to the Secretary-General's proposal to provide more funding for the Resident Coordinator System for the regular budget. While the increase of $53 million from the regular budget provides a thin but essential cushion of funding, it still falls far short of providing an adequate and sustainable base. We still count on Member States to provide voluntary contributions. We rely on the UN System Development Group to continue to pay their portion of the cost sharing, and we look to both to dutifully pay the levy. We are preparing a comprehensive review of the Resident Coordinator System, as requested by the General Assembly for the 81st session, informed by robust data and analysis. This recalibration exercise will ensure the RC system is optimally capacitated and structured. In 2024, because of a lack of funding, only 33% of RCOs were fully staffed. The intake of candidates for the RCHC talent pipeline had to be paused, with implications on the diversity of the expertise available in the future. The Resident Coordinator System still remains our most efficient investment to support the sustainable development of countries at scale. Resolving the long-term shortfall, which was nearly $80 million in 2024, must be resolved to enable it to fully deliver on the mandates that you have given. There are other lingering challenges which we must overcome. The early findings of the system-wide evaluation on country configuration and derivation are stark, and you will hear from the Executive Director of the UN SDG System-Wide Evaluation Office tomorrow. The need for action will be clear. Dialogues on UN teams configuration have set to transformation— to transform country-level presence or expertise, and entities' programming instruments are still not fully derived from the cooperation framework. Over the course of this year and next, we will work with Member States, and the UN System Development Group entities to right this ship. I count on your leadership in this Forum and in the Governing Bodies to ensure that we're all pulling in the same direction towards a more tailored, cohesive and coordinated support, ensuring that each entity plays to their comparative advantage. We're working to ensure that the tools and structures are optimally aligned with the needs of countries. The forthcoming reviews of the business models of the UN SDG entities, the management and accountability framework, and the cooperation framework guidance provide a critical window to ensure the UN system is aligned in structure and process and guided by clear accountability lines with a much more efficient response. Excellencies, we're now entering a decisive window, the second half of the 2030 Agenda. And there is absolutely no time to lose. In the Pact for the Future, Member States recommitted to advancing the SDGs. Let us strengthen the system to enable us to deliver on this commitment. And let us ensure that the UN Development System receives the support it needed to deliver for the people it serves. And let us invest in the UN Development System as a matter of shared responsibility and a strategic necessity for a sustainable future that leaves no one behind. Thank you.

Thank you, Vice President, and thank you very much to the Deputy Secretary-General. I have the honour to deliver this statement on behalf of the EU and its Member States. The candidate countries North Macedonia, Montenegro, Albania, Ukraine, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Georgia, as well as Armenia, aligned themselves with the statement. The EU, as a strong supporter of the UN Development System reform, welcomes the findings of the 2025 UN Development Coordination Office report. This report highlights both progress and challenges as we approach the 2030 deadline to achieve the SDGs. We would have 3 comments. First, the Resident Coordinators are central to a reformed UN Development System and essential for delivering a coordinated, joined-up, and integrated country-level support in line with national priorities. The report shows that RCs are effectively convening governments, donors, and UN country teams, shaping integrated and evidence-based solutions, and achieving better collective results. RCs are driving SDG progress, coordinating new sustainable development frameworks, responding to crisis in a nexus approach, and influencing policies. The data is telling: 90% of governments reported integrated policy advice from the UN, 88% saw increased RC leadership, and 98% of cooperation frameworks aligned with national priorities. The EU and its member states welcome the opportunity to engage with RCs during the OAS, and we would encourage better alignment of the RCs' yearly meeting in New York with the OAS to allow stronger interactivity and coherence. Second, we urge member states, UN agencies, entities, and other development partners to continue supporting the UN Development System and empowered, effective, and impartial RCs. As part of the discussions on the UN reform, and as we discussed yesterday, the EU still believes that a more unified multilateral presence is needed in country and at regional level to deliver on objectives. However, challenges remain, and this brings me to my final point. The system is working to maximize efficiencies, saving $6.2 million through cost avoidance and advancing shared services. We encourage the system to continue identifying efficiencies and to analyze how the Resident Coordinator System will be impacted by the UNHCR reform process. If any information is already available on this, we would welcome it. The EU and its Member States have been at the forefront and continue to advocate for adequate, predictable, and sustainable funding of the Resident Coordinator System, with a funding mix comprising the levy, cost-sharing, and assessed contribution, as was agreed in the QCPR and eventually in the budget. Since 2019, the EU and its Member States contributed more than $300 million. In addition, despite improvements, stronger coordination among agencies is still needed to work and deliver as one UN, and we look forward to the Board meetings to discuss this too. The EU will continue collaborating with RCs, UN country teams, and EU embassies to ensure successful implementation of the UN cooperation frameworks. Thank you.

Mr. President, Madam DSC, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the Group of Least Developed Countries. First, I wish to express our sincere appreciation to the Deputy Secretary-General and the UN SDG Chair for the comprehensive report on the Development Coordination Office and the Resident Coordinator System. We acknowledge with satisfaction the progress made in strengthening the RC system 6 years into the repositioning of UN development system. The group believes that Resident Coordinator System fully supports our efforts to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals and implement the Doha Programme of Action for LDCs. We commend the Development Coordination Office for its ongoing support to UN country teams in least developed countries, particularly for adapting assistance as per the unique needs of these countries. We are encouraged to note that 98% of host governments agree that UN activities through the cooperation frameworks are closely aligned with their national development needs and priorities. This alignment is crucial for the effectiveness of UN system support and country ownership. On behalf of the Group of LDCs, I wish to emphasize that effective implementation of the Doha Programme of Action remains— our top priority. Its success hinges significantly on a well-coordinated and effective UN Development System support at the country level. We recognize and value the RC system's support to LDCs in several critical areas. We acknowledge the RC system's contributions in advancing integrated policy advice aligned with the SDGs, DPOA, and the National Development Strategies. In many LDCs, RCs have facilitated high-level coordination on critical issues including climate change adaptation, food security, and economic transformation. We appreciate the RC's key role in supporting the graduating LDCs in preparing for smooth transition. The report highlights how RCs have spearheaded initiatives for LDC graduation, helping integrate transition strategies into national development plans. This support must be further strengthened as we work toward enabling 15 additional LDCs to meet graduation criteria by 2031. Similarly, the Joint SDG Fund and other pooled funding mechanisms have been instrumental in catalyzing resources for LDCs. However, we note with concern that the share of UNCTs that successfully mobilized global pooled funding dropped to 70% in 2024 compared to 82% previously, and this trend needs to be reversed. We highly value the RC's network and their participation in our national focal points meeting and all the relevant meetings to share their insights and recommendations to further strengthen the implementation of DPOA in LDCs. Excellencies, as we move forward, I would like to offer the following recommendations from the LDC perspective. First, we call for explicit and tailored support to LDCs for integration, implementation, and monitoring of DPOA in LDCs. We request the RCs to support the national focal points of DPOA on DPOA in each LDC to support in preparing the national reports on the implementation of the DPOA. This is especially significant as we prepare for the midterm review of DPOA to be held in 2027. Second, we strongly call for sustainable and adequate funding for the RC system. Third, RCs should facilitate enhanced South-South and triangular cooperation to supplement North- South cooperation, as emphasized in DPOA. And finally, the RC system should establish dedicated mechanisms to support graduating LDCs during their preparation and smooth transition periods, including enhanced capacity for data collection and resource mobilization. To conclude, Excellencies, our group reaffirms its commitment to working closely with the RC system to advance our development priorities, and I thank you for your kind attention.

Thank you, Mr. President. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the Group of Landlocked Developing Countries. We thank the Deputy Secretary-General in her capacity as Chair of the United Nations Sustainable Development Group for the report on the work of the Development Coordination Office and her— and for her continued leadership of the UN Development Coordination Reform. The LLDC Group welcomes the strong positive feedback received by the Resident Coordinator System in the report. Resident Coordinators have played a key role in ensuring that UN support is closely aligned with national development strategies and specific country contexts, including in developing— including in landlocked developing countries. We underline the centrality of the Resident Coordinator System as a cornerstone of the reformed UN development architecture. Through empowered leadership and coordination, the RC system has delivered more coherent, efficient, and integrated support to LLDCs. Responding to the complex and cross-cutting nature of our development challenges. We commend the Development Coordination Office for its continued support to UN country teams in LLDCs, particularly in reinforcing regional coordination and tailoring support to landlord contexts. We see particular value in the integration of the Programme of Action for LLDCs into into the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks. We also welcome the DCO's engagement with regional commissions and multilateral development banks to ensure that UNCTs can draw on regional expertise in addressing infrastructure, transit, and trade challenges. The Group encouraged the continuation of targeted surge support and technical backstopping for LLDCs, particularly in crisis and post-crisis contexts. We valued the contribution made by RCIS in coordinating multi-stakeholder platforms around transit corridors, trade facilitation, and digital access. We acknowledge with concern the continued dependence on voluntary contribution to sustain the Resident Coordinator System. Predictable, sustainable financing is crucial to ensure continuity of supporting in LLDCs, which often have limited institutional capacity and heightened vulnerability. We also highlight the need to further strengthen data-driven policy support, including through the use of multidimensional vulnerability index and other tools that reflect the specific challenges of landlocked geography. On the later— latter, LLDCs remain highly expecting to be included in the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index. In the current context of institutional challenges within the United Nations, including the ongoing discussion under the UN 2.0 and UN80 initiatives to streamline mandates, the LLDC group expresses deep concern regarding any potential reduction in mandates of UN offices that are instrumental in addressing the specific needs of LLDCs. At a time when tailored support is more critical than ever, the group stresses that such mandates must not only be preserved but actively strengthened. The complex and persistent development constraints faced by LLDCs exacerbated by geographical isolation, limited market access, and vulnerability to external shocks require a reinforced UN presence with, with the expertise, resource, and flexibility to respond effectively. We urge that instead of diminishing the capacity of these offices, the UN system prioritize and expand targeted assistance for LLDCs. Ensuring that the unique needs of our group remains in central focus of the development agenda. Finally, we reaffirm our support for the UN development system reform and encourage the Development Coordination Office to continue enhancing its ability to deliver responsive regionally linked and nationally owned development support in LLDCs. The Resident Coordinator System is not only central to this vision, but indispensable to the effective realization. Thank you.

The Africa Group welcomes the detailed insights provided in the report on the functioning and evolution of the Resident Coordinator System and the Development Coordination Office. The growing alignment with national priorities and the enhanced convening power of Resident Coordinators in our countries. We are also encouraged by the continuous efforts to ensure that the Resident Coordinators are equipped with the right profiles and skill sets tailored to the specific needs of programme countries. Good morning, and thank you for giving me the floor. Good morning, Deputy Secretary-General. We would like to join the statement made by the G77, and in our national capacity, we would like to thank you for presenting the report, thank the Chair of the UN SDG, the report on the Development Coordination Office and the Resident Coordinator System, and we value this dialogue in particular. More than 5 years after the reform of the UN development system, we recognize that significant progress has been made in terms of coordination, joint planning, and alignment with national priorities. The report reflects specific results which were achieved by many countries thanks to a structure which is more consistent, empowered, and ground-focused. For Uruguay, the system of resident coordinator has been a key ally in the implementation of the cooperation framework for 2021 to 2025, a reflection of our national priorities as well as sustainable development. But I can also say, and as I've taken part in previous processes, The resident coordinator system in Uruguay has been successful from the very beginning. It's made it possible to set up a cooperation agency. It has made it possible to develop public policies in a joint fashion. And it's been a model that has led to a greater management of governance in our country. We value the strategic accompaniment and the coordination between agencies. Which the agencies have found in Uruguay in the last 30 years. It has strengthened intersectoral approaches in areas such as climate change, gender equality, and digital transformation and energy transition. We also highlight the support given in the development of new financing mechanisms, and it's made it possible for Uruguay to carry out the first combined census of Latin America, We also highlight the participatory development of the cooperation framework with clear goals and alignment with our public policies, which has favored a shared vision of sustainable development. In this context, we acknowledge the effort made by the Development Coordination Office to promote a culture of results, to strengthen accountability, and to improve operational efficiency. But of course, there are still challenges such as financing gaps, the fragmentation of resources, and difficulties in a consistent multiannual planning, and that's why we believe it's important to move towards a model of financing which is sustainable and predictable for the Resident Coordinator System. Within the framework of the UNAD Initiative, we believe that any organizational reform must incorporate experiences of the Resident Coordinator System as well as the country team in contexts such as ours, which require integrated solutions as well as innovative public policies. Vice President of the ECOSOC, Deputy Secretary-General Amina Mohammed, thank you for the comprehensive presentation. Secondly, we must shift the agency's incentives. I strongly believe that UN agencies are at their best when they are true to their core mandates and play that out through integrated approaches. And thirdly, we must continue to work for sustainable financing for the RC system, for lean but solid RC offices. Norway has fully supported the SG proposal for assessed contributions and were pleased to see that partially agreed last year. And let me add that I am impressed by the leadership shown by the Deputy Secretary-General channel on creating an even better development system. Thank you.

Vice President, Madam Deputy Secretary General, Excellencies, colleagues, we'd like to thank the Deputy Secretary General and her team for their continuous commitment to the UN development system. Cuba aligns itself with the statement made by Iraq on behalf of the G77 and China, and by Palau on behalf of the AOSIS. We value progress made in the Resident Coordinator System in strengthening consistency within the development system and in its growing ability to provide support to the national priorities of our countries. However, it's disturbing to see that 6 years after the system repositioning, We have not been able to guarantee adequate, predictable, and sustained financing for a function which is considered a pillar of the reformed system. Cuba reiterates its appeal to developed countries to comply with their historic commitments in providing support for development. The insufficient financing levels cannot in any circumstance justify that we transfer the financial burden to developing countries, nor that we reduce the operational impact of agencies on the ground. Doing so would be a twofold injustice—first of all, because countries of the South are not responsible for the current financial deficit, and secondly, because it's precisely the developing countries who depend the most on the support of the agencies in order to move towards sustainable development. And we also— we would also reject any attempt to increase the coordination tax on projects on the ground to finance the system, insofar as that would reduce the amount of money that would be available for the benefit of local populations. This situation goes against the principle of common but differentiated responsibility and would render meaningless the commitments it had taken on in the QCPR relating to the operational activities of the UN Development System, and would also render meaningless the 2030 Agenda and the Funding Pact. Reducing the impact on the ground due to budget limitations would directly affect the credibility of the UN system. The value of the Resident Coordinator and the country team is measured by their ability to offer concrete, coordinated solutions which are in line with national priorities. If this capacity diminishes, not only would development be affected, but also the trust among member states. In times of crises and restrictions, the response must be more cooperation and more solidarity. If not, we will be giving up on our promise to leave no one behind. Thank you very much.

Vice President, my dear sister distinguished DSG. I thank Sister Amina DSG for the comprehensive report and for her continued leadership in advancing a more coherent, accountable, and effective UN Development System, fully aligning myself with the statements of the G7 and the African Group, adding the following: We appreciate the details in the report on the functioning and progress of the RC system and the Development Coordination Office. We acknowledge the progress achieved by the RC system in bringing together the breadth of the UN policy expertise to support programme countries and enabling greater engagement by specialized and non-resident UN entities. We're also concerned that the Resident Coordinators are enabling more integrated UN country— we're encouraged that the RCs are enabling more integrated UN country team responses and facilitating more access to to pooled funding and financing SDG solutions, in addition to advancing operational efficiencies. We're concerned about the impact of the protracted funding shortfall by the— on the ability of the RC system to deliver on its mandate and the expectations of programme countries. The gap between the needs of developing countries and funding for sustainable development has been growing. Regrettably, the continued decline in availability of sufficient funding for UN Development System and the increased earmarking in funding for UN entities has a negative impact on operations in programme countries. At a time when international community is facing unprecedented and interconnected challenges, the importance of preserving and strengthening Multilateralism has never been more urgent an imperative. We call on all Member States to recommit to the spirit of international cooperation, solidarity that lies at the heart of the UN. Egypt has been supportive of the UN Development System reform from the outset and will continue to do so, and we hope that the UN80 Initiative and reforms it's bringing that wonderful spirit of raising efficiencies will not be at the expense of the great successes of the RC system. Africa needs an operational and well-funded RC system, I submit, distinguished Vice Chair. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Egypt, and now I give the floor to Canada, to be followed by Morocco and Costa Rica.

Thank you, Mr.

Vice President. Uh, Madam Deputy Secretary-General, Canada thanks you for your continued leadership and commends Resident Coordinators and UN country teams for their continued efforts to advance the 2030 Agenda. We would also like to take this opportunity to reaffirm our strong commitment to a well-resourced and empowered RC system, which remains central to delivering effective integrated support to countries to achieve their Sustainable Development Goals. In this regard, the Government of Canada is pleased to have recently disbursed its 2025 core funding to DCO for the RC system, thereby maintaining our level of support under our multi-year agreement alongside this year's assessed contribution to the UN overall, which we have paid in full and on time. Sustained, predictable, and reliable funding is critical to maintaining momentum and achieving lasting results. We welcome the 2024 report on the UN Development Coordination Office and the Resident Coordinator System and note the progress made to increase UN coherence at the country level. At the same time, we recognize that there is more work to be done to further strengthen the role of the RC at the country level. Emphasizing the importance of the Resident Coordinator to ensure accountability and transparency across the UN development system is essential. We welcome the inaugural report of the System-Wide Evaluation Office and encourage further progress towards the achievement of a more strategic, accountable, and responsive UN system. We also encourage the continued expansion of results-based reporting, including at the outcome level, which demonstrates clear linkages between funding and SDG outcomes. In addition, we welcome the Secretary-General's reflections on strengthening collaboration across UN entities to advance gender equality and human rights. The UN's normative functions, particularly in promoting the rights and empowerment of women, are more vital than ever. This work must remain a core, system-wide priority, underpinned by clear accountability mechanisms. And in this respect, the RC can play a vital and strategic role by identifying and leveraging opportunities to elevate normative issues that are crucial for accelerating progress at both the country and regional levels. Finally, we support further reforms that enhance impact, efficiency, and coherence. It is critical to ensure strong alignment between the ongoing UNDS reform agenda and emerging initiatives such as UNAID and the Humanitarian Reset. Advancing this coherence at the country level requires that the vision of an empowered and well-supported Resident Coordinator be fully realized. Thank you.
I thank the Representative of Canada, and now I give the floor to Morocco, to be followed by Costa Rica and Brazil.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President, Madam Deputy Secretary-General, Excellencies. On behalf of my delegation, I would like to express our thanks and appreciation to Madame DSG for the insightful briefing on the report and for her unwavering advocacy and leadership in advancing a more coherent, effective UN Development System. We join other delegations in commending the quality and evidence-based findings of the report, which offer both compelling records of progress and a forward-looking call to do more and better for for the years ahead. We'd like to make 4 brief points. First, Morocco welcomes the fact that the RC system has shown tangible results in driving a more effective, coherent, and nationally responsive UN presence on the ground. The data provided in the report on the strong alignment with the— of the cooperation frameworks with national priorities is a clear signal that the spirit of the GA Resolution 72 Resolution 279 is being realized. Two, as we look ahead for UN80, Morocco underscores the importance of anchoring development coordination and funding for development activities at the center of this transformation. UN80 is not only a commemoration, it is a decisive opportunity to shape a modern and responsive UN. Three, in the last mile of the 2030 Agenda, It is paramount to build on the gains of the UNDSR positioning. The system effort now shall concentrate on achieving impact on the ground for the acceleration of the SDGs. We would like here to join the call made yesterday by the Philippines on behalf of the LMG mix to establish a dedicated focal point for middle-income countries within the UN development system as mandated by the 2024 QCPR for a tailored support for middle-income countries. Fourth, as numerous UN entities embark now in the development of their new strategic plan, we look forward to the governing bodies that they ensure that those plans are forward-looking, build on the progress achieved over the 6 years of the UNDSR positioning, and incorporate the necessary flexibility to align programming with national needs and priorities. We welcome the efforts done in terms of upscaling profiles and skill sets for the RC profiles and RCOs based on values of dedication and impartiality, and upscaling capacities for the evolving context of each country and region. Finally, the sustainability of this progress depends on predictability and sustainability of the funding. While we welcome the GA recent decision to increase the share of regular budget of the RC system, the ongoing reliance on unpredictable funding continues to jeopardize the stability. We look forward to a sustainable solution for the funding of the RC system. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Morocco, and now I give the floor to Costa Rica, to be followed by Brazil and Denmark.

Gracias, señor vicepresidente.

Thank you, Vice President. Costa Rica acknowledges the valuable support provided by the Resident Coordinator, Alegra Baiocchi, and her office. Allow me to highlight 3 key points. First of all, it's necessary to ensure that the reform, particularly the outcomes of the UNAID Initiative, is consistent with national and regional priorities. In Costa Rica, the Dialogues for the Future, which engaged more than 2,000 stakeholders from across all sectors, as well as the preparatory dialogues for the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, demonstrates that direct and effective participation of all sectors is essential for UN initiatives to truly respond to the needs of our populations. Secondly, the work of Resident Coordinators is key to overcoming operational fragmentation and delivering concrete results at all levels. The joint programs funded by the SDG Fund and coordinated by the Resident Coordinator's Office have proven to be valuable tools in reducing agency fragmentation and mainstreaming an intersectional approach to gender and localizing the SDGs. These good practices must become the norm, not the exception. Costa Rica recognizes the leadership of Resident Coordinator Alegra Bayoki in facilitating integrated, innovative, and timely responses, as demonstrated during the management of the regional human mobility crisis, the— in the future dialogues, as well as the national consultations for FFD4. Third, it's essential to move toward a fair financing model, one that goes beyond GDP per capita. This model must be sufficient, predictable, and equitable. It also requires strengthened resource mobilization capacities through innovative mechanisms, particularly in areas such as climate finance, debt sustainability, and ocean protection. Chair, by presenting our third voluntary national review on the SDGs last year, Costa Rica demonstrated substantial progress in nearly 60% of the 2030 Agenda indicators. The Resident Coordinator's Office in Costa Rica has played a fundamental role in this achievement. Thank you.
I thank the representative of Costa Rica and now I give the floor to Brazil, to be followed by Denmark and Armenia.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. Brazil aligns itself with the statement made by Iraq on behalf of the G77 and would like to make some very brief comments on our national capacity. Brazil holds the view that implementation of the RC system has been an important step towards a more efficient and coherent UN development system and commends the UN SDG Amina Mohammed for her leadership in this area. One of Brazil's long-standing priorities, shared by many member states, has been the development of robust methodologies to assess the efficiency and effectiveness of the UNDS. The report before us is a welcome step in that direction. At the same time, we note the continued lack of more granular, country- and sector-specific data. We also need more regular mechanisms for oversight by member states, which would help ensure the system's further improvement and responsiveness to national needs and priorities. We stress the importance of strengthening the link between planning and implementation. Cooperation instruments such as the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks should truly serve as catalysts for joint programs rather than declarations of intent. While progress has been made, it's concerning that 21% of UN entities still do not derive their national program from such frameworks. We encourage DCO and the UN SDG to advance the revision of strategic guidance tools, including the management and accountability framework, and to further strengthen coordination and accountability mechanisms. As the Resident Coordinated Systems undergoes review, it's key to tailor its profiles and capacities to reflect the diverse realities of member states. In the case of middle-income countries such as Brazil, there is a particular need for specialized technical support to foster transformative public policies and promote innovation in development financing. We welcome the report's recognition of the IRC's role in responding to emergencies and natural disasters. A recent example is the severe flooding that affected the state of Rio Grande do Sul in 2024. The prompt and effective engagement of the Resident Coordinator in Brazil was instrumental in enabling timely and effective UN response on the ground. We are grateful. And we are confident that continued reform will contribute to strengthening national capacities and supporting meaningful progress toward the implementation of the SDGs. Thank you.
I thank the representative of Brazil, and now I give the floor to Denmark, to be followed by Armenia and Switzerland.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. Deputy Secretary-General, thank you for your leadership and presentation both yesterday and this morning. Denmark aligns itself with the EU statement and today just some brief national comments. The relevance of the UN development system is determined by its impact and results at country level, and we welcome the Secretary-General's UNAID reform initiative, including the designated UNAID/UNDS clusters. In launching UNAID, the The Secretary-General encouraged all of us to turn our eyes to the future and to ask how the UN can be the most effective and responsive organization that it can be. Kindly allow a few remarks in this regard. Firstly, the 2024 report offers valuable insight into recent results and into some of the barriers encountered to the 2018 UNDS reform. Denmark acknowledges the positive outcomes achieved, particularly the high level of satisfaction by host countries, 98% of whom report that UN at country level effectively responds to national priorities. Yet challenges do persist. One-fifth of UN country team entities still do not base their programming instruments on the cooperation framework. Like also mentioned by you this morning, Madam Deputy Secretary-General. Prompted by the SG's question of how the UN can be the most effective organization that it can be, rather than dwelling on existing ways of working, allow me to point to two issues or questions. Firstly, what systemic changes might result from the UN80, which could and hopefully can once and for all strengthen RC leadership in the UN Country Team? And secondly, what deeper structural adjustments might UNAID enable that can shift business models and incentive systems so that all UN entities prioritize cooperation frameworks and collaboration around joint objectives and results? Your reflections on this, Honourable Deputy Secretary-General, could help us to inform Member States' UNAID engagement. We are also keen to listen to host governments' UNAID expectations for the UNDS. Secondly, lack of funding in an era of shrinking development budgets is identified as an obstacle multiple times throughout the report. As articulated in the UN Funding Compact endorsed by Member States last clear funding flows express mutual commitment. The Funding Compact Monitoring Framework importantly notes the need for common standards on visibility and recognition, and we hope that that can also ensure continued support for the UN Development System. We warmly welcome action to proceed with development of such standards. Thank you so much.
I thank the representative of Denmark. Now I give the floor to Armenia followed by Switzerland and Sweden.

Distinguished Vice President, distinguished Deputy Secretary-General, I would like to express appreciation for the insights of the report on the Development Coordination Office, showcasing the crucial role of the UN Development System in accelerating the SDG implementation at the country level. Armenia recognizes the pivotal role of the DRC system in better coordinating the activities of the UN country teams ensuring improvement in accountability and transparency, as well as advancing the operational efficiency and need-based programmatic activities of the UN. We believe that Resident Coordinators are also uniquely positioned to support the governments in fostering inclusive engagement with a wide range of stakeholders, facilitating coordinated action and mobilizing the necessary resources to accelerate the progress towards the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals. Currently, the Government of Armenia, in close coordination and cooperation with the RC office, is elaborating its second UN Development Cooperation framework carried out through an inclusive and participatory approach with the objective of having an action-oriented and fit-for-purpose document. Taking this opportunity, we would like to commend the effective work of the RC in ensuring that the priorities identified within the UN SDCF are coherent, complementary, and strategically aligned with our national priorities and needs. Mr. Chair, the reforms of the funding model of RC system remains of crucial importance. To address the challenges deriving from the lack of adequate, sustainable, and predictable funding. In the light of Secretary-General's UNAT Initiative, we would like to underline that the efforts of enhancing overall efficiency, coherence, and responsiveness of the UN development system must not come at the expense of the proper and effective delivery of its programmatic assistance. In conclusion, let me reiterate Armenia's readiness to continue to advocate for leveraging the strengths and expertise of the UN entities in supporting the implementation of the Agenda 2030. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Armenia. And now I give the floor to Switzerland, to be followed by Sweden and Philippines.

Mr. Vice President, Madam Deputy Secretary-General, thank you very much for your report and your briefing. We are impressed by the progress made and in particular the positive feedback on RCs and the RC system by host countries. The current funding crisis really risks pulling the UN operational system apart if competition for funding is put before coherent and coordinated UN support to countries. Three things therefore seem imperative. Firstly, the cohesion of UN country teams, and in extension the impact the operational system can achieve in countries, hinges on the RC system. We need to further strengthen it and sustainably fund it. Also, the authority of the RCs cannot only depend on their personal power to convince. RCs need more formal authority. Secondly, we need to make use of all funding instruments that fight competition among agencies, such as pooled funds, MPTFs, and in particular the Joint SDG Fund. Thirdly, within country teams, the use of shared services and common back offices needs to go much, much further. The same is true at the regional and global level, and here we expect some bold moves. Last but not least, all of us Member States, donors and host governments alike, need to ensure that our efforts at the country level reinforce our commitments to to an effective UN operational system. A system that is unique and whose legitimacy, values and mandates are precious. Thank you.

I thank the representative of Switzerland.

And now I give the floor to Sweden, to be followed by Philippines and United Kingdom.

Thank you, Mr.

Vice President, Madam Deputy Secretary-General Amina. Sweden fully aligns itself with the EU statement. Just a few points in my national capacity. We appreciate your leadership and dedication in leading the UN Sustainable Development Group. We also thank the Development Coordination Office's support to RCs and UN country teams. Sweden remains committed to the RC system, evident in our consistent funding and engagement with the Sustainable Development Group entities governing bodies. We are concerned that country programming programming instruments are not fully derived from the cooperation framework, showing— slowing the UN Country Teams' configuration. We recognize our role in shifting business models and incentives, a priority in today's dialogue with UNDS Executive Heads and upcoming Executive Boards. We commend the efforts to strengthen a context-based UN presence and recalibrate DCO and RCO structures, including reviewing surge capability— capacities for crisis response. A flexible UN with skilled RCs who adapt to evolving needs is crucial. The reported $596 million in efficiency savings for 2024 is impressive, reflecting progress in common premises, back offices, business operations, and shared services. However, with 130+ country offices, further savings are possible. Only 4 common back offices exist, which we believe should be a standard for all offices. So our question to you is, how can member states support the UN Development System at country level to accelerate this progress? On information sharing and resources— resource mobilization, RCs are not sufficiently involved in outreach to funding partners, so we will encourage embassies and development cooperation colleagues to fully integrate RCs into their dialogues with UN country team members. And finally, we deeply appreciate the Resident Coordinators and their teams leading joint UN efforts on the ground and supporting governments in achieving the 2030 Agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals.

Thank you very much.
I thank the representative of Sweden. Now I give the floor to the Philippines, followed by United Kingdom and Zimbabwe.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. We align with the statement of the G77 and China and have the following comments in our national capacity. I thank the Deputy Secretary-General for the comprehensive report on the DCO and RC system. The report shows that the RC system continues to evolve in the right direction, to be part of the solution, working with our countries as we strive to achieve the SDGs in accordance with national development priorities. We appreciate the collaboration with the UN Country Team in the Philippines on disaster risk reduction in the face of natural disasters and on our advocacies for middle-income countries and South-South cooperation, including in the Asia-Pacific region, among others. Reform and recalibration are ongoing processes. We hope that in the process of reform, substantive and tailored support is not sacrificed, particularly for the specific challenges and transition pathways of middle-income countries whose successes can create ripple effects in the world economy. We see the RC system as central to the UN delivering as one on the ground. The new generation UN sustainable development cooperation frameworks have played an important role in this regard, yet we continue to see some operational challenges in aligning various country program documents of UN agencies and look forward to further improvements. The idea of one common document among UN entities as mentioned by the DSG yesterday, is very interesting and could be one way forward. We also see room for improvement in terms of reporting and monitoring of implementation of the Sustainable Cooperation Frameworks, as well as equitable geographic representation in the appointment of RCs. In the face of growing uncertainties and volatility, we need to preserve and strengthen the sustainable development pillar of the United Nations through adequate and predictable funding, especially regular and unearmarked funding. Likewise, leveraging other sources of development finance, such as from the private sector, and working on long-term investments, in particular digital transformation, sustainable infrastructure, and human capital development, are urgently needed. The UNDSNRC system, with the leadership of the DSG and DCO, must be empowered by member Member States to continue their important work and implement the QCPR. In conclusion, delivering on development is one of the key tests to rebuild trust in the UN and multilateralism. Forging partnerships and strengthening the UN's capacity to make a difference is our collective way forward. Thank you.
I thank the Representative of the Philippines and now I give the floor to United Kingdom. To be followed by Zimbabwe and Indonesia.

Thank you, Vice President, and thank you, Deputy Secretary-General, for presenting this report. Firstly, the UK welcomes the funding agreement reached by the UN General Assembly's Fifth Committee at the end of last year. This is, however, a temporary arrangement, and I hope we'll be able to work towards a permanent solution to funding the RC system, one that takes into account a more tailored setup suitable to the context in question. Your report provides an important moment for us to reflect on the value of the RC system, the extent to which the 2018 reforms have been implemented, and what more is still needed to fully empower Resident Coordinators. It remains the UK's view that the role of the RC is central to bringing coherence and coordination to of the UN system, ensuring the UN development system is working closely with host governments and other development actors to accelerate delivery of the SDGs. From our perspective, a key outcome of UN80 must be to empower the RC system to deliver its full potential. So to achieve this, we believe RCs should, inter alia, do more to drive coordination and hold agencies, funds and programmes accountable, including on remaining within their mandates. As part of that, we'd like to stress the continued need for the cost-sharing funding arrangement. Second, have greater authority to ensure the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework is used to guide all agency and donor activity. And third, in consultation with host governments,— and as part of the cooperation framework process, determine the configuration of UN country teams. I'll conclude with two questions. First, with just 33% of RC offices fully staffed in 2024, what is being done to prioritize recruitment for in-country vacancies? And second, how can UNAT be used to further empower the RCs? I thank you.
I thank the representative of United Kingdom, and now I give the floor to Zimbabwe, to be followed by Indonesia and Lao People's Democratic Republic.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. We wish to thank the Deputy Secretary-General, Madam Amina Mohammed, for a briefing, and also thank the UNSDG chair for the comprehensive your report on the Development Coordination Office and the Resident Coordinator System. The Resident Coordinator System is not just a coordinating mechanism, it's the backbone of our collective action at country level, bringing together all UN agencies and strengthening cooperation between the UN country teams and governments. In the case of Zimbabwe, the Zimbabwe UN Sustainable Development Framework has contributed to structured and predictable cooperation and has enabled effective channeling of UN assistance in support of the government economic blueprint, the National Development Strategy 1, including the implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals. Going forward, it is our hope that with the ongoing review under the UNAID Initiative Cluster on Development, the Resident Coordinator System will be further strengthened with the concomitant allocation of appropriate resources. We reiterate that any cost-saving measures should be equitably implemented without prejudice to ongoing development programmes, in particular in developing countries. Zimbabwe reiterates the importance of aligning UN support with national development programmes. It is our expectation that Resident Coordinators will continue facilitating collaboration between governments and the United Nations and ensure that programmes and initiatives complement government efforts to transform the lives of citizens. In Zimbabwe, the first cycle of our National Development Strategy is coming to an end this year, with the current cycle of the Sustainable Development Framework ending in 2026. Zimbabwe commends the UN system for providing technical support as we finalize the elaboration of the second cycle of our development strategy, with work at an advanced stage to develop the successor Sustainable Development Framework which will be aligned to NDS 2. Mr. Vice President, one of the major hindrances to the achievement of the SDGs is inadequate funding. Due to unilateral coercive measures, countries such as Zimbabwe do not have access to concessional international funding. While domestic resource mobilization remains a valuable tool to secure funding, resources remain insufficient, compounded by debt overhang, which often compels countries in debt distress to redirect resources from development initiatives towards servicing debts. We call on Resident Coordinators to redouble efforts to access pooled funds to support SDG implementation in their duty stations. In conclusion, Zimbabwe reiterates its support for the strengthening of the Resident Coordinator System. We look forward to continued collaboration with the UN system to advance development, including the implementation of the SDGs. Thank you.
I have thanked the representative of Zimbabwe and now I give the floor to Indonesia, to be followed by the Lao People's Democratic Republic and Ireland.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. Indonesia aligns itself with the statement of the G77 and China delivered by Iraq and would like to make the following statements in our national capacity. We extend our appreciation to the Secretary-General for her presentation on the report. Indeed, the UN development system, particularly through the UN Resident Coordinator system, plays a vital role in supporting the member states in making progress with their SDGs achievement. In this regard, Indonesia wishes to emphasize 3 key points. First, closer coordination between governments and UN Resident Coordinator is essential. Strong collaboration with host governments is crucial to maximizing the benefits and impacts of development programs. This coordination ensures that projects are effectively aligned with national priorities while also reinforcing national ownership and participation at all levels. Second, enhancing the focus on project impacts to guarantee lasting and concrete benefits. Development programs must be optimized deal for tangible and long-term improvements in community level. The UN Resident Coordinator in this regard plays a critical role to be government's stronger supporter in development through coordinating and ensure a more synergized UN country team. Lastly, we must seize every opportunity to scale up support. Last year, we collectively adopted the Pact for the Future, which calls for enhanced support for the UN development system, including the RC system. We recognize that RC system must be more strategic, responsive, accountable, collaborative, and integrated in supporting development priorities of member states. In this regard, support for a more sustainable and predictable funding is also critical to ensure the UN RC system deliver their mandate. To conclude, Mr. Vice President, Indonesia remains committed to support the UN development system, including the UN Resident Coordinator System, and stand ready to enhance collaboration, working hand in hand in ensuring concrete implementation of Sustainable Development Agenda. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Indonesia, and now I give the floor to the Lao PDR, followed by Ireland and Russian Federation.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President, Madam Deputy Secretary-General. My delegation aligns itself with the statements delivered by the Groups of 77 and China, LDCs and LDCs, and wishes to add the following remarks in our national capacity. We thank Madam Deputy Secretary-General for presenting the UN SDG Jazz Report on the Development Coordination Office Resident Coordinator System. The Lao PDR recognizes the importance of the RC system as the key pillar of the reformed UN development system. RCs continue to serve as critical enablers in orchestrating the efforts of the UN country teams, ensuring that support is delivered in a coordinated, coherent, and contextually nuanced manner, aligned with the national development priorities.. In the face of persistent funding constraints and increasing demands for accelerated SDG implementation, the strategic relevance of the RC system has only deepened, underscoring the indispensable role in delivering integrated, impactful development assistance at the country level. In the Lao PDR, the RC has played an instrumental role in fostering synergies among UN entities is advancing an integrated approach to operationalizing the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework. Looking ahead, we encourage the RC system to continue evolving and scaling its support to ensure that it remains optimally responsive to our country's development trajectory. In this regard, allow me to underscore the following areas. It is essential to maintain a strong and agile RC system that can effectively align the UN development system support with our national development priorities, steering the UN country teams' function in a coherent, more integrated, and result-oriented manner. Second, enhanced coordination both within the UN development system and with international financial institutions must be a top priority to unlock the means of implementation, particularly through mobilizing adequate, predictable, and sustainable financing that empowers the RC system to meet escalating and evolving demands. Third, the UN development system must remain attuned to the particular vulnerabilities of countries in special situations by tailoring context-sensitive support and delivering through reinforced and inclusive partnership. This task is essential to advancing the implementation of nationally owned development strategies, as well as the dedicated Programme of Action for LDCs and LLDCs. I wish to conclude by calling for the UN Development System to remain fit for purpose and fully equipped to respond to today's challenges and accelerate the implementation of the 2030 Agenda. Thank you.
I thank the representative of the Lao People's Democratic Republic and now I give the floor to Ireland, to be followed by Russian Federation and Germany.

Thank you, Vice President. Ireland aligns itself with the statement of the European Union and would like to add the following in a national capacity. Thank you, Deputy Secretary General, and to DCO for your leadership, for the report, and for this interactive dialogue. As we stated yesterday afternoon, Ireland is a very strong supporter of a capacitated, accountable and enhanced RC system, driving coherence and effectiveness and efficiency at the country level. This is a system that belongs to all of us and which, thankfully, we now all contribute to through the regular UN budget. This funding, of course, needs to be enhanced. Ireland is also happy to continue to provide voluntary funding of €1.5 million per annum for the RC system. Allow me in particular, as Brazil did, highlight the role of RCs in fragile contexts, operating under very difficult situations, responding to crises, breaking down silos, coordinating humanitarian responses, and often in contexts where, very sadly, international humanitarian law is being seriously eroded by actors. The role of RCs in transitions also needs to be brought out—when peacekeeping missions are phasing out, for example, and departing. And that's where critical support is required. I remember meeting the RC in Mali about a year and a half ago. There was a peacekeeping mission there of $1 billion per annum. His discretionary budget, when they had left, was around $100,000. It doesn't make sense. More broadly, though, the evaluation evidence and your report shows clearly the improvements in coherence, integrated policy advice, and convening through the reinvigorated RC system. However, improvements can still be made in fully coordinating UN delivery of operational activities at the country level, and for that we need streamlining of management and reporting, clear roles and responsibilities, strong accountability and incentives for collective analysis, planning and, importantly, action. As we have heard, the UN80 Initiative should be a moment for us to push through and further ahead with this reconfiguration. I'd like to ask about the ways in which, therefore, country cooperation frameworks, rather than tending towards perhaps being catch-all documents, could instead enable more focus and targeting and enabling of RCs to have a stronger management. And I should add, by the way, that we as donors also need to ensure that our funding and engagement provides incentives for such instead of concentrating on islands of excellence or our own national flags. Thank you.
I thank the representative of Ireland and now I give the floor to Russian Federation to be followed by Germany and Cambodia.

Mr. Chair, Russia recognizes the importance of the function of the Resident Coordinator system in efficiently and coordinated responses from the UN development system to the development challenges at the country level. However, we traditionally underscore the need for appropriate recognition of the work of the UN development system, which carries out the programmatic results on the ground. It's important for the coordinating functions of Resident Regional coordinators, including at the global and the— we traditionally underscore the need to recognize the work of the UN Development System agencies in delivering programmatic results on the ground. It's important for the coordination functions of Resident Coordinators, including at the global and regional levels, to be strictly aligned with mandates in the General Assembly resolution on the reform of the UN Development System. It's important to prevent duplication of functions, not only between various agencies and the UN development system, and also between the agencies and the Resident Coordinator System. Specifically, substantial capacity on areas such as financing for the SDGs and statistics already exists in UN agencies and should not be reproduced in the Resident Coordinator System. Sustainable financing for the Resident Coordinator Financing system is certainly important to support its efficient work. However, we need to note that without providing adequate financing to UN development agencies, there will simply be nothing to coordinate. And without an adequate level of unearmarked contributions, agencies will not be able to maintain and provide to country teams valuable technological expertise. Given the decline in ODA, the priority should be put on Development Goals and the process of reforming— in the process of reforming the system, the focus should be shifted from procedural and institutional issues to tangible programmatic results, including at the country level. And we have a couple of questions in connection with the report. First, we'd like to hear what is meant by recalibration of the Resident Coordinator System. Will the member states be involved in consultations in this process? Secondly, paragraph 70 of the report talks about a 1% levy not only on tightly earmarked contributions but also on voluntary resources. This runs counter to the agreed parameters for financing the RC system, and I'd like to know whether or not that's a mistake or what was being referred to here. Furthermore, every year we talk about the need to provide member states with the methodology that's used to calculate the savings and resources, and that hasn't happened yet. We'd also like to receive information about the activities of the Special Advisor of the Secretary-General on reform. That's Jens Vandel. And we'd also like to hear about the regional level of resident coordinator systems, which is not very well developed in many people's opinion, including the opinion of resident coordinators. How could this system look in the context of the calibration of the system?
Thank you. I thank the representative of Russian Federation. Now I give the floor to Germany. It will be followed by Cambodia and United States.

Thank you, Chair. Madam Deputy Secretary-General, Excellencies, Germany aligns itself with the statement delivered by the EU. Let me express Germany's gratitude and appreciation to the DSG, the DCO, and their teams for their work in general and specifically for presenting this comprehensive report. In just 6 years since the reformed RC system was established, it has made significant strides in strengthening coordination and generating efficiencies. Equally important, RCs have proven their value to lead the UNDS normative engagement at country level, as we heard yesterday from several RCs. The RC system is an essential is part of the solution to the current challenges the UN faces. The UN SDGs Chair's report rightly calls it a launchpad for deepening reforms. In fact, many of the objectives set out by the SG in his plans for UN80—namely streamlining operations, reducing duplication, and strengthening collaboration while upholding the UN's normative work, can be achieved through a strengthened commitment to implement the UNDS reform, both by Member States and by UNDS entities. We must, however, be candid about remaining challenges. Let me point out three. First, the RC system remains chronically underfunded. There is a clear gap between what it what it is mandated to achieve and what it can realistically achieve with current resources. This year Germany has paid its assessed contributions in full and on time and has provided additional voluntary contributions to the RC system. What are your plans to address this challenge in the short and medium term? Second, we were concerned we were shocked to learn that in 2024, only one-third of RC offices was fully staffed. According to a 2024 OIOS evaluation, capacity constraints are particularly severe in complex settings. How can the staffing challenge be addressed? And third, we note a disconnect between the intended strategic use of the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks and their often superficial application, with 21% of UNCT entities not deriving their programming instruments from it. Thus, we welcome the recalibration initiative by DCO and kindly request further information on this. To conclude, Our collective investments in UNDS reforms are already paying off tremendously and must therefore be consolidated and furthered. Germany stands ready to continue its support. Thank you.
I thank the representative of Germany and now I give the floor to Cambodia to be followed by United States, India, and Nigeria.

Mr. Chair, on behalf of Cambodia delegation, we appreciated very much the chair report on the Development Coordination Office and the resident coordinator system. As I am a former Director General of the National Institute of Statistics of the Ministry of Planning of Cambodia, I would like to share my knowledge on the UNSD support the National Institute of Statistics over the period of 2017 to 2021 on the SDG monitoring project. I thank the representative of Cambodia. And now I give the floor to United States, to be followed by India and Nigeria.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President, and thank you, Madam Deputy Secretary General. In the report prepared for this session, the United States notes that the UN will undertake a recalibration of the Resident Coordinator System, including the the Development Coordination Office itself. We would welcome you sharing more details on this recalibration now if they're available. Additionally, we suggest regular member state briefings on this recalibration, similar to the briefings you offered in fall of 2023. To help prepare the Secretary General's report on the RC system. In this recalibration and review, we encourage the UN to adopt another approach considering country context— and limited resources. Can you share some common back office success stories with us? Thank you.
I thank the representative of the United States. Now I give the floor to India, to be followed by Nigeria.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President, Madam DSG. India recognizes the vital role that the Resident Coordinator System plays as the linchpin of the reformed UN development system. We appreciate the candid assessment provided in the UNSG Chair's report on both the achievements and challenges faced in 2024. We are encouraged to see that 88% of host countries acknowledge increased Resident Coordinator leadership and push for common results. We also appreciate the progress in ensuring diversity in the Resident Coordinator cohort, with 53% now being women and 51% from program countries as of March 2025. We are particularly encouraged by the significant advancement in digital transformation within the RC system. This initiative aligns well with India's own prioritization of digital solutions for development challenges. However, we note with concern several challenges highlighted in the report. The funding situation for the Resident Coordinator system remains precarious,, with total funding for the Special Purpose Trust Fund amounting to only $202.1 million at the end of 2024, leaving a gap of $79.7 million against the full RC system budget of $281.8 million. While we welcome the General Assembly's decision to provide additional funding of $53 million from the regular budget, we recognize that the continued reliance on unpredictable voluntary contributions may impact the ability of the system to fully deliver at the scale and pace expected by member states. As one of the largest contributors among program countries to the UN development system, India recognizes the importance of supporting the Resident Coordinator System. We have consistently advocated for more predictable funding mechanisms that reduce reliance on year-to-year voluntary contributions. India takes particular note of the report's reference to the establishment of a country-level pooled fund with a specific window on South-South cooperation in India. Reflecting India's commitment to South-South cooperation. Cross-pollination of best practices is a vital task of the UNRC, and India looks forward to continue working with the Office of Resident Coordinator in transmitting the positive stories and takeaways from our vibrant cooperation. Thank you.
I thank the representative of India, and now I give the floor to Nigeria.

Mr. Vice President, Madam Deputy Secretary General, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. We wish to also add the following remarks in our national capacity. Nigeria appreciates these reforms with the UN Development System, which in our view have enhanced the leadership and operational effectiveness of country teams and have allowed for better translation of global commitments into impactful country-level actions., which is crucial for nations like Nigeria that face unique development challenges. Mr. Vice President, with its overarching objective to eradicate poverty in all its forms and dimensions.
