I thank the representative of Nigeria. That concludes the list of speakers. We have heard 30 interventions, both from the Major Groups and individual member states, after which I invite the Deputy Secretary-General to respond to these comments, questions. Thanks to your time discipline, we got the Enough time for the DSG to respond. Thank you.

Thank you very much, Vice Chair. I want to just express really my deep appreciation of the constructive, as always, comments that you give us and the immense amount of support that we've had from all of you, not just for the UN Resident Coordinator System, but for the UN country teams that work together with the Resident Coordinators across the world delivering on development in very complex situations, and today you do know that they are— the avalanche of expectations from them, and at the same time the whole defunding that has happened and the pushback against some of the core values that we hold is a difficult, very difficult space to be working in. A lot of anxieties from our member in the countries that we are present as to what are we going to do and how are we going to go about it. And of course, over the last few weeks, you have seen the SG's response in how to cope with that and the three steps to trying to engage with this building on what we have already been doing for the last seven years, but also recognizing that more needs to be done and perhaps out of this crisis we can profit from it and we can come out of it better rather than worse. I'm sure that we can, and I see UN80, as SG does, as about more and not less. Yes, the funding is going down, but if we have a repositioning, a reset of how we respond, being more efficient, being more representative, being more responsive to the needs, then I believe that funding will come back to the development system and it won't just be about less, less, less, and less. I believe that we will get more out of what happens at the country level, particularly if our FFD IV meetings in Sevilla go well and people recognize that the means of implementation financing, not just the development system, but countries who are trying to attain the 2030 Agenda, removing those barriers that are necessary and creating more fiscal space at the country level, where we as a UN Development governance system can then respond with the necessary policy support that will enable those resources garner more, but also be used much more effectively and efficiently. And remembering, we are in very difficult contexts. There are conflicts around the world that are different in each one of our regions. Our ability to help to resolve them is varying from some that have been there for a few months and others that have been there for years. The climate crisis, the humanitarian crisis, it goes on and on. It does not let up, and yet we are not putting enough into the development response that is required. So difficult for us to do, and I know that we are all stretched of funding, particularly those that have made the commitments to ODA, seeing less of that. And, you know, the competition that this creates, it really gives me great concern because it is about choiceless choices. You have to fund and find the resources for a development footprint which is represented in country teams to support countries. That's what we've done for 80 years and we need to continue to do that. Yes, more efficiently, more productively, and we can do so much more to turn that around, but also the coordination. Mechanism that we put in, and it was very deliberate to separate that in 6 or so years ago when we were trying to have a division of labour. So it is not competition and neither should it be seen as one size fits all, even across the development system. And so I hope that as we are considering much of what we report back to capitals on the efforts being made by the UN system, that we're also advocating in our capitals, across our capitals, in our networks, for this to be more about less, because we cannot contain what we say is the backslide in not attaining the SDGs by 2030. We have to get the money in there, and we have to do it faster to scale, but of course, much better. A number of questions that have been asked and issues that have been raised— I think one of the most important is how we work together across the three pillars. And I think that we've tried to strengthen that. Of course, we've spoken to the political side of the house where we are triple-hatted—how do we become much more of an integral part of that management and response so that countries are getting all sides of the needs that are there? We have the responsibility for development, there is a humanitarian hat that we wear, but the political side of the house are the partners that we work with, the senior partner in many of those countries., and we have to work like this, and we continue to try to make sure we have the resources and the capacities to do so. They are much more different from a standard setting where we're just looking at an RC, not even double-hatted. So as the reforms are coming across the bow, particularly the humanitarian reset, the 10-point agenda, just yesterday and the day before, we have all our RCs, HCs, with Tom Fletcher, Head of OCHA, in Istanbul working on this and making sure that there are no gaps, because of course, as you reduce your footprint, there will be an ask. There has to be a transition. In that transition where suddenly offices are closed and staff are paid off, then we— what is the connection there and helping governments to fill that? In many cases, governments are trying to respond, not to the full gap that has been created, but they are stepping in for that emergency. Emergency response when we lose humanitarian footprint. It causes tensions in those countries, tensions within those that are working around that space, our NGOs and ourselves. A lot of questions around the efficiency— I mean, we have a number of tools. You have been part and you have accompanied us on all of the tools that we've created. Over time. And one of the— one of those tools is the MAF, and the MAF itself, I think, after the system-wide evaluation and the many other consultations that we've had, it's clear that as we are reviewing it, that it is a MAF that has to— that has to be much sharper and leaner, and of course more user-friendly, eliminating any of the ambiguities that we've had. And this is feedback that we've we've had from the system, but also, of course, the end users at the country level. So the MAF itself undergoing sufficient and, I think, deep revision to make sure that it is more effective, and we'll be happy to share what we're doing with that. Other tools that we've used: the cooperation framework. And I think, you know, when I first came to the UN, my I mean, my first interaction with an UNDAF, which is what it was called then, and even then the cooperation framework that came after, was really a collection of ideas and priorities and investments that were not bad in and of themselves. Every single one of them would have made an impact in someone's life, so I think we have to be true to that. But they were so far apart from what the priorities of a country were, and my country was one of the the first I looked at, having been a cabinet minister, to sit there in the UN office thereafter and say, 'Really, okay, I don't recognize the priorities of my country. I recognize that these are issues in my country, but these are not the priorities.' And so I think that what we did with the cooperation framework over the years was really try to pull our UN country team and their country project documents to align, and I said this yesterday, they are not aligned in most cases. But this is not all the— if we're going to apportion blame, I wouldn't do it on the UN country teams, the agencies, funds, and programs. They are shaped by the funding that they get and the priorities and what is needed to be seen by taxpayers to the issues they think are important to them. And I think we have to find this balance where it is clear that most countries today, if not all, understand where the shoe is pinching. And so their priorities are important and we need to get behind that. And if there's— you asked where can we help? Well, I think the help of member states and the boards. Now, you have a checklist on the reforms and I think that that, by and large, is— we see a lot of forward leaning and it's not enough, but at least it's in the right direction. But I do think we need to look at the boards at how we are how we are responding to that. Board meetings probably never long enough because these are detailed documents that have gone through months of preparation, and it is why, you know, I said, well, I mean, there are— yes, I said yesterday, let's think of the one document. That's in an ideal situation, provided that one document is about country priorities, is about country ownership, and we don't start negotiating country priorities and their ownership. That's a risk that we all come to. When we're looking to fund development in our countries. And I think it has to be thought through, so I think, you know, let's look at what is the best approach to try to address this with the cooperation frameworks that will come up for discussion within the course of our work. You gave us a resolution in December last year, which we are faithful— I apologize if the language is— that we've chosen is is not helpful, but really it's a response to that resolution that asks us to do that office-by-office review and constantly tells us how— what a bad idea the one-size-fits-all is. And I think, you know, here again we have a lot of work that is going on to respond to that. Clearly, we have to have an internal look at how this is evolving in our states. I mean, there are many— hundreds 132 offices that we have to go through and look at the multi-country offices, look at all of what it means and to see what sort of options could we have, run through them and not just talk about them, but actually work through them and then, of course, we will come back to you with it because it does have to come in the report. It does include DCO. I mean, DCO was the first when we stood up this reform, a really conscious decision that if there was resident representation, it does not sit in New York. This is too far from where the problem is and where the support to RCs need to be. So that's where we are. In fact, the RC regional meetings that I've had to date, if not for that regional competency, we wouldn't have been able to get all of those RCs together, the preparation that happened with them so that in a coherent way they could give us a picture of what those challenges were that country teams the governments were facing, that how we could do better in responding to some of the issues that you've picked up today. So I think, yes, we need more support and more strengthening of those offices and a calibration of the balance between what we support here at headquarters and what goes to the regional and country levels. So you will see— it will have, as I said, impact.. We have to ask the question: where we have a development footprint as a country team, is an RSC necessary or not? We believe they are necessary, but we're asking about the configuration of those teams. How many of those teams can be non-resident? How many of those teams have to be on the ground? And I think here it should be determined by the priorities of a country and the expertise that they require. Finding that expertise and delivering it to countries requires for us also to look at the systems of interoperability. You know, with the best will in the world, some of our agencies will want to exchange the experts they have to send a surge capacity to a country like Chad, for instance, that requires specific multidisciplinary support, but it's easier to go get a consultant than to do that. And so we have to find what are the rules that are preventing this? I'm told that technically it's not a problem, but we just have to get through this with the— in the Secretariats, with the management side of the house, and this, of course, is where member states have great sway. In agencies, funds, and programs, it's a little easier because they're reporting to their boards and we can see more flexibility, but we are taking each and every one of these up in the regions within countries, and we see that lessons learned from the multicountry offices, the first thing the multicountry offices did for us in the SIDS was improve the capacity and the capability of the expertise that we sent. Before that, it was well below, and I just want to thank the SIDS for pushing us— AOSIS for pushing us and telling us, 'You're not giving us the right capacity to be able to deal with our issues. You're not understanding us.' I believe Indonesia was the second country that pushed us for that,— and thank you for it. I think we are doing much, much better than we had done before. So, cooperation frameworks recalibration. On the mix, I'm asking for the support for that, of course, for all LDCs, LLDCs. We try to support each and every one that has these complex settings and different needs, so that ask for a tailored support. It's more than just the RC office. Which of course can't carry more than it can because even what it does carry can't get paid for, but the UN country teams, we need to look at the profiles of our UN country teams, the capacities of them, because we are not operational in the RC system. We are coordinating and we're convening and we're passing the operational piece to our country teams. If they don't have those capacities, then it's going to be very difficult for a country to see that that's met.. And often this is not the case. Again, an inability to, I guess, to implement the Funding Compact, which asks for far more core funding to allow us to do that. This is something that we would plead with you. Please, we need more core funding to go to our agencies' funds and programmes. We cannot— it's not one or the other. We have to have a coordination system with a country team that can perform around the framework of the common— the common cooperation frameworks that we provide against the 2030 Agenda. So in the case of MICS, I know that we do have some representation, but our representation for what we've been able to do to support is more recently, I think in the Philippines, we did have a meeting, is the regional DCO office. That's where we try to search support too so that they, together with the resident coordinators that are in those countries, to take a more coherent and structured approach to agreements that you have had. Funding concerns, I mean, these continue to be there. Frankly, I hear from every one of you that this is a good investment. Certainly, the evidence and the data that comes back to us, as far as we can get it, tells us that this is is a good return on investment. I think we still have to make the case. We still have to do more to effectively show you what that value proposition is, because there are still unanswered questions, you know, 6, 7 years later. Sometimes it's the turnover of the people that we have, so we just have to do a better job and to make sure that you're satisfied with the responses we give and that you can make those arguments back in capital or across your your networks and partners. The FFD4, of course, I hope will provide much more support to find that fiscal space, but also to support the efforts that we make with the 6 transitions and the 4 capabilities we think ought to happen. I see in the FFD4 negotiations that there is a push there for capabilities and capacities for domestic resource mobilization. I think that's very, very important because we do need to support that. Will we be able to see financing coming in for the UN system to support our country teams, as well as direct financing going into the countries themselves? Let me see where else you had some— ah, the efficiencies initiative. Oh, goodness gracious me. What can I say? I mean, I try to— you know me, I'm not the diplomat. I wish I was, but in the case of the efficiencies, it is a massive disappointment. Massive. We spend 7 years here trying to do what you asked us to do. Of course, you serve in the boards, and so therefore you know what your agencies' funds and programs are doing. It certainly isn't efficiencies.— not on premises, not on common back offices, not on general services. Do we have a case of success? Well, one of you mentioned you got 4. Do you know how many I asked for, committed to, and 7 years later I have 4, but I asked for 50, which is less than what I had expected. And so, you know, it's not that we can't do it. We surely can, and that's why I say that the disruptions that we have now I'm pretty sure that UNAT is going to fix this, because it has to. It has to. We cannot continue to see some of these efficiencies in the offices that we have, not with premises, not with common back offices. We should be doing what is happening in Nairobi. It works. And even then, it took us years to get that done. So we need to shake up— we need your help, we need your help in the boards. Ask the questions of these efficiencies. Today, we fortunately have two co-chairs of what we say is the BIG, the Efficiency Initiative of the Development System. It's co-chaired by UNFPA and UNOPS. These are incredible members of staff of those organizations who are taking this up and telling us as it is, and even suggesting that you think 20 you can get through, well, that's a really big lift. So anything you can do, whatever member state we're talking about, if you can get me 132 offices that tow rope, I'm open for that. But I can tell you it's taken us 7 years to go from 50 to 4, and that really— someone should be held accountable for that, because quite frankly, the efforts that were made— and I do say by agencies, funds, and programmes, some really cool agencies out there who have done it— but we have to take the lot with us. In many countries, we are 26, 27 agencies, funds, and programmes.. And we have to think about this and how this helps. I see UN80 as an accelerator for a lot of what we want to get done. In the first instance, we're having to deal with the shock of sudden funding drops and, of course, building on the reforms that we have, how can we be more efficient? On the second, you know, the mandate review, and that will show many things, even to the development system itself. Itself. There are mandates there for implementation, and that I think we will consider. And when we come to the thinking through, once we've cleaned up house and we've seen how we can work better together across the agencies, funds, and programs, yes, we'll have to look to see whether you need 42 agencies, funds, and programs. Perhaps we don't. These have come over the years. 2025, 5 years to the SDGs, and we will get another set of goals. Is this how we ought to be represented? Representing ourselves in the country without losing the mandates, without losing the thematic priorities and thrusts of what those resolutions have put to get to the SDGs. I suspect we will be many less in terms of structures, but we will consolidate better, we will work together better with what happens on the humanitarian side, what happens on the peace and security side, and it does have to speak across the three pillars.. And we have to make sure at the centre of this is human rights, that we're delivering on those rights, because that is what keeps us going every day, is that we're looking at all those that are being left behind, and they are billions in doing so. So efficiencies, we can give you informal briefings on what the— what it is that we intend to do to get back on track.— this was shared at the UN SDG just before the CEB meetings in Copenhagen, and it does take on to continuously. The system-wide evaluation report was also very good in helping us to see how we could be much better at doing so. So, yeah, that's on our efficiencies. Our country back offices— again, a lot of questions on the efficiencies and the alignment between the two. Tailored support— let me say that what we are doing in many of our country offices today, you know that we have the UN 2.0, it's the Quintet of Change. For me, the most important bullet of that Quintet of Change is the behavioural change. The behavioural change that we have to go through in every one and facet of this organization is huge. And again, it's because over the years, you know, we have layered and layered and layered the things that we need to do. Now we need to get back to the core and we need to facilitate that at the country level. We are, of course, now in a new era of technology. It's incredibly helpful. It speeds up everything that we do. It gives us a much better leadership function in a team representing the government. When you do have data, you have innovation, you have AI, and you're able to do foresight analysis, giving trends to countries based on the data that we have as a system. This is really important. We, for instance, have given instructions to our country teams who are way behind, you know, our resident coordinators are way behind on this when we evaluated, but they have until the end of of the year for every single one of them to be working with 2.0. We started that work even in the retreats to use the technology. It's quite difficult to jump in the deep end, but they can swim once they start. FFD, right. There was a question about international staff. Today, what we have— Let me just say we are— each region is different depending on what we are expected to have. In many of our middle-income, high-income countries, we just have the RC. The rest are national staff. But in countries where those capacities are not there, then we're having more, 2, 3 international staff. But today, the figure that we have— where have I got that I don't know, it's about 456, I think, of the 1,250-odd international staff that we have, so it's about 35%, and we're still looking at that. That's something that the SG has asked us also to have a look at. What we don't want is to reduce the capacities available. There should always be an exit strategy. You have 3, 4 international staff, how are they building up capacity when you come for the renewal of that post? Is it sufficient? Have we found sufficiently capacity in the country that can replace it? We do so. We're not fixated on it, but we can do better, but we don't want to reduce capacities that are needed in countries for that. Again, important. A question asked about our special advisor, Jens Vandahl, on the work. I mean, last last year he started that work just to do— I think a number of member states have said to us, 'Have you evaluated what you've done with the reforms and what needs to be done?' He was in the middle of doing that work when, of course, UNAT was born, and so we are aligning and calibrating his work. He's working with Guy Ryder in the task force, the Secretariat, and ensuring that we are building on reforms that happen. Happy to give you responses or have him brief you on that,, but he is working together with us, together with Guy Ryder, in the UN AT Secretariat, so we don't lose the work that we've done and the evaluations that he started to do with that. Again, I think that is what we had from there. The US, you asked for— I think I've spoken to the big, I've spoken to the one-size-fits-all, and the international staff. Have I forgotten something? Accelerating filling vacancies, good grief. Yes, okay, this is another one. I mean, if there's no liquidity, the freeze comes. When the freeze comes, there's just no way to do that. And by the time you get back to trying to fill those capacities, right now, mixed messages, we don't have money for it, you know, what do we do? You as member states have given us the $53 million and we will use what we can of that, bearing in mind what we've said about the efficiencies, and we have already started to fill those posts as they are prioritized to give that response. I mean, we are asking countries also to tread water, because as we are seeing a reduction in the resourcing and the footprint of the UN, programs are suddenly changing. Our response is suddenly changing, where we are double-hatted, and so very quickly, don't rush into a cooperation framework now, because we could look very different in the next few months. So extend it. And the same with staff. Of the staff that we really need right now, we need to put them there, because actually they have to help member states grapple with what is happening with the support from the international system. And it's not just the UN. This is also with our IFIs, this is also with our international— the foundations that are there in country. This is affecting everyone, so there is a reset and recalibration, but we are continuing to go as fast as we can with it. The reforms, as we looked at them, Jens was not just looking at development reform, he was looking at the peace and security and he was looking at the management. And now that the RC system is in the Secretariat, there's a whole lot of other issues that come with it and how to make sure that the management part of our house is efficient enough to support us to do the work that we need in the recruitments. Much easier when we were with UNDP. But then you come over, you— this is the system we're in. This is some of the recalibration that has to be done to make that much easier. Question again on the development emergencies? Well, context is very much— It's very much a part of what we are looking at when we said the recalibration of the capacities in, in, uh, in RC offices and RCs, and whether we are bringing together or not. But those complex settings certainly need much more attention, and we have got already quite a bit of work that we've done on that. In the next couple of weeks, we might have something more that we can share with you., but we don't want to do the, as they say, the chicken before the egg or the egg before the chicken. But the context, the complex settings have been ones that we have, that we've had a lot of work to do.
